controls.statement: The problem being solved and intended users are documented.
Release scope, non-goals, and deferred features are explicit.
Every feature has testable acceptance criteria.
Critical user journeys are ranked by business and user impact.
Critical journeys include onboarding, normal use, error recovery, account recovery, cancellation, and deletion where applicable.
Product behavior for unavailable dependencies and partial failure is specified.
Product behavior for empty, malformed, incomplete, stale, or conflicting data is specified.
User-visible terminology is consistent.
Pricing, entitlements, quotas, billing rules, and plan limits are unambiguous.
Cancellation, refund, reversal, dispute, and undo behavior is defined.
Expected customer support obligations are documented.
Service hours, maintenance expectations, SLOs, SLAs, and contractual commitments are aligned.
The launch does not make claims that the implemented product cannot substantiate.
Product management has accepted the final behavior of critical journeys.
Define measurable launch success criteria.
Define measurable launch failure and rollback criteria.
Define adoption, conversion, quality, reliability, support, and safety indicators.
Define the observation period before declaring the launch complete.
Define who has authority to pause, continue, expand, or roll back the launch.
Establish expected traffic and customer cohorts.
Establish whether the launch is internal, private, regional, percentage-based, invitation-only, or public.
Ensure marketing, sales, support, and operations use the same release date and scope.
Ensure help content, screenshots, pricing pages, documentation, and legal text match the released behavior.
Ensure customers are notified of breaking changes, downtime, migrations, or changed data use where required.
Every production service has a named business owner.
Every production service has a named engineering owner.
Every data set has an accountable data owner.
Every security-sensitive component has a security contact.
Every third-party integration has an owner.
Every operational dashboard, alert, and runbook has an owner.
Every scheduled job and background process has an owner.
Ownership remains valid during holidays, leave, and personnel changes.
Escalation paths include primary, secondary, management, security, privacy/legal, and provider escalation contacts.
Offboarding and role-change processes remove or adjust access promptly.
Classify confidentiality impact.
Classify integrity impact.
Classify availability impact.
Classify privacy impact.
Classify financial and fraud impact.
Classify physical, psychological, societal, and user-safety impact.
Classify regulatory and contractual impact.
Classify reputational and customer-trust impact.
Identify likely attackers, abusive users, insiders, compromised accounts, automated agents, and accidental failure sources.
Identify foreseeable misuse and abuse cases, not only intended use.
Maintain a release-specific risk register.
Give each risk an owner, likelihood, impact, treatment, evidence, and review date.
Record accepted residual risk and the person authorized to accept it.
Review high-impact assumptions with independent subject-matter experts.
Verify that launch scope remains inside the organization’s risk appetite.
Ensure risk exceptions cannot remain open indefinitely.
Ensure compensating controls are tested rather than merely described.
Map applicable security controls to a recognized verification standard.
Map applicable privacy controls to legal and organizational requirements.
Map accessibility requirements to the selected WCAG conformance target.
Map operational controls to SLO, incident, continuity, and recovery requirements.
Map contractual controls to customer, processor, provider, and partner agreements.
Identify conflicts between product requirements, legal requirements, and technical controls.
Document how conflicts were resolved and who approved the resolution.
Apply separation of duties to high-impact changes and approvals.
Periodically review whether the selected control level still matches the app’s risk.
Maintain an up-to-date system-context diagram.
Maintain component and deployment diagrams.
Maintain end-to-end data-flow diagrams.
Mark trust boundaries explicitly.
Mark Internet-facing and externally reachable interfaces.
Mark administrative and support interfaces.
Mark where authentication and authorization decisions occur.
Mark encryption and decryption boundaries.
Mark where sensitive data is collected, transformed, stored, cached, logged, exported, backed up, and deleted.
Mark all third-party data transfers.
Identify every stateful component.
Identify every asynchronous boundary and queue.
Identify common dependencies and shared failure domains.
Identify single points of failure.
Identify control-plane dependencies needed during incidents or recovery.
Identify circular and hidden dependency chains.
Document required consistency, ordering, durability, and freshness properties.
Document architectural invariants that must never be violated.
Document expected failure behavior for every critical dependency.
Record material architecture decisions and rejected alternatives.
Update diagrams whenever the release changes data flow, trust, topology, or dependencies.
Verify the documented architecture against the deployed environment rather than assuming documentation is accurate.
Perform a threat model for the actual release scope.
Include all trust boundaries, actors, entry points, data stores, and external systems.
Model spoofing and identity attacks.
Model unauthorized modification and integrity attacks.
Model information disclosure and privacy attacks.
Model denial of service and resource exhaustion.
Model privilege escalation.
Model repudiation and inadequate accountability.
Model business-logic abuse.
Model insider and compromised-administrator threats.
Model dependency and build-system compromise.
Model tenant-escape and cross-customer attacks.
Model automation, scraping, spam, fraud, and economic abuse.
Model recovery-system and backup attacks.
Model support-channel and account-recovery social engineering.
Convert identified threats into requirements and tests.
Revisit the threat model after material design or scope changes.
Obtain independent review for high-value or high-risk systems.
